summary:
The world is building data centers for super intelligence, SI for short. They are huge and they go up fast. Companies announce them. Nobody outside can check.

SI Orbit is an open web app that checks with NISAR, the new radar satellite of NASA and ISRO. NISAR passes the same ground every 12 days and sees through cloud and at night. Flat fields look dark to radar. Walls and steel look bright. So new construction lights up, and we measure it in hectares.

The app shows 96 SI data center campuses on a night globe. Pick a site and watch every radar pass as a slow time-lapse. Other NASA and ESA satellites show what the land was before and what changed around it. A measure tool lets anyone check any plot.

At Meta's Hyperion site in Louisiana, radar confirms about 190 hectares of new construction since February 2026. That is about 260 soccer fields.

Anyone can check a public claim with open data. Companies announce. Radar checks.
details:
What it does

SI Orbit is a web app that tracks how fast SI (super intelligence) data centers are being built, using NASA's new NISAR radar satellite. It starts with a globe that shows 96 SI data center campuses in 12 countries. When you pick one, the app flies down to it and plays a slow time-lapse of every NISAR pass over that site, with a counter that adds up the new construction in hectares. You can zoom in and out with the mouse or with two fingers on a touch screen, turn on a "build calendar" that colors each patch by the month it first showed up, and compare the radar with a normal satellite photo.

Each site also has an Impact page. It uses other NASA and ESA satellites to show what the land was before, how much vegetation is gone, how much brighter the site is at night and whether the surface got hotter. There is a Measure tool where you draw a box anywhere on the picture and it tells you what happened on that piece of ground and when. All the numbers can be downloaded as CSV or JSON.

How it works

Radar sees flat ground as dark because the signal bounces away, and it sees walls and steel as bright because the signal bounces back. So when something gets built, that spot turns bright and stays bright. For every 10 m square we compare each new pass with the first passes. If the square gets about twice as bright and stays like that on every pass after, we count it as new construction. We do the same thing on the land around the site, to make sure we are not just counting crops or wet soil. At Hyperion about 13% of the site area gets counted, and less than half a percent of the land around it.

What we found

Hyperion (Meta, Louisiana): about 190 hectares of new construction since February 2026, which is around 260 soccer fields. In 2021 most of this land (82%) was farmland, and the site is now about 84 times brighter at night than in 2023.

Project Jupiter (New Mexico): about 110 to 160 hectares.

Madison Mega Site (Amazon, Mississippi): about 67 hectares.

Why it matters

Companies announce these projects, but people who live nearby, journalists or city planners have no easy way to check how big they really are or how fast they grow. With SI Orbit anyone can look it up using free public data. It is also a simple way to show what NISAR can do to people who have never seen radar data before.

What is creative about it

Radar images are hard to read, so we turned them into one number and a time-lapse. We also compare the radar with other satellite records (night lights, vegetation and ESA's Sentinel-1 radar) and show how many of them agree, which is 4 out of 4 at Hyperion. The app also tells you when nothing changed, which we think is just as useful.

What we considered

We tried not to claim more than the data can show. Radar can't tell what a building is used for, so the names and owners come from a public list by Epoch AI. Flat roofs and paved areas look dark to radar, so we miss them. Construction that started before the first NISAR pass is not counted. Things like soil moisture, rain and air quality are only shown as background for the area, because we can't prove the site caused them. Out of the 15 sites we tested, 6 had too much change in the land around them, so we don't show a number for those.

Tech we used

Data processing: Python 3.12 with NumPy, SciPy, h5py, pyproj, Pillow and earthaccess. It reads NISAR L2 GCOV files (HDF5) from the Alaska Satellite Facility through NASA Earthdata, and writes JSON files and WebP images for the app.

Other data: Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, Landsat and WorldCover through the Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC API, which runs on Azure. Night lights come through NASA GIBS and climate data through the NASA POWER API.

App: JavaScript, HTML and CSS with no framework. The radar view and the charts are drawn on HTML5 Canvas, the globe uses WebGL with three.js, and the touch gestures use pointer events.

Hosting: a static website on Microsoft Azure.

Tools: Claude Code as an SI assistant, and Microsoft Edge for testing.
